ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: The Brook, The Hill And The Forty-Five Years Of Silence

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: The street you just got on the bus in is called **Lækjargata — Brook Street.** There is no brook. It is still there, running under the tarmac, and in January it is the reason the ducks in the city pond have anywhere to swim.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: That hill is **Arnarhóll**, and the man on it is **Ingólfur Arnarson**, who the tradition says was Iceland's first settler. The tradition — and say it as a tradition, because that is what it is — has him throwing his **öndvegissúlur**, the carved pillars from either side of a chieftain's high seat, over the side of the ship and settling wherever they washed ashore. They came in below this hill. **What archaeology can actually pin down is different and better:** there were people here **before the ash layer dated to AD 871, give or take two years.** The statue is by **Einar Jónsson**, and it was not a gift from the state — the **Reykjavík craftsmen's guild** paid the **40,000 krónur** and unveiled it on **24 February 1924.** Arnarhóll was a working farm until the **1820s.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: Now the brook. **Lækurinn** ran from the pond down to the sea, the old town grew up on the west side of it, and the street was named **Lækjargata in 1848.** In **1911** they put the brook in a culvert and paved over it. **It is still flowing under us.** And here is the good part: the pond — **Tjörnin** — freezes in winter, except for one patch. Guides will tell you that is a natural hot spring. **It is not.** It is **warm overflow from the city's hot-water system**, coming out at the old brook outlet by Iðnó. One warm corner, and every duck in Reykjavík standing in it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: Off to the right on **Austurvöllur** is the **Alþingishúsið**, the parliament, built **1880 to 1881** by the Danish architect **Ferdinand Meldahl**, out of stone quarried up the hill in **Þingholtin.** And this is where you correct the guidebook. **Alþingi was founded at Þingvellir, traditionally in 930** — the oldest parliamentary institution in the world by date of foundation. **But it is not the oldest continuously running one, and Alþingi does not claim to be.** It was **shut down by royal decree on 6 June 1800** and did not sit again until **1 July 1845.** **Forty-five years of silence.** That gap is the whole reason the Isle of Man gets to argue about this.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík
en: Last one on the skyline: **Hallgrímskirkja**, the concrete tower you can see from most of the city. **About 74 and a half metres** — the parish's own leaflet says 73, and I am not going to pretend that is settled. It was designed by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, and the shape is meant to be **columnar basalt, mountains and glaciers** rather than anything churchy. Building started in **1945** and it was consecrated on **26 October 1986** — **forty-one years.** Guðjón died in **1950** and never saw it. The statue of **Leifur Eiríksson** out front is older than the church behind it: **a gift from the United States** for the **1930 millennium of the Alþingi**, formally handed over on **17 July 1931.**

en: 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: Look ahead — the whole peninsula opening up in front of us.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: A **constructive plate boundary** and a **mantle hotspot** overlap nowhere else on Earth. Iceland exists because both happen in the same spot.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: Today's route is basically a guided tour of a crack in the planet. Mind the step.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: Weather pivot (if it's socked in): "You will not see much of the peninsula this morning, and that is fine — everything I am about to show you is at your feet rather than on the horizon."

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: We're driving onto the only stretch of mid-ocean ridge on Earth that pokes above the sea. Most geologists only ever see one on a diagram. You're about to spend a day standing on it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: The whole peninsula is a **UNESCO Global Geopark** (**2015**) — one of only a handful of places where a **mid-ocean ridge climbs above sea level.** Normally the North American/Eurasian plate boundary sits **2 km down** on the seafloor. Here you can walk on it, and later today you will.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: The park protects ~**825 km²** of lava, geothermal fields and rift. **Four to six linked volcanic systems** run through it — Reykjanes, Svartsengi, Fagradalsfjall, Krýsuvík, Brennisteinsfjöll, Hengill — out of ~30 Iceland-wide. We will be inside four of them before lunch.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
en: Iceland is a **double engine**: a spreading **plate boundary** sitting on a stationary **mantle hotspot.** The oldest rock anywhere in Iceland is only **fifteen or sixteen million years** old — and out here on Reykjanes it's a tiny fraction of that. The hotspot beneath has been burning for at least **60 million.**

ctx: gloss for the name "Reykjanes" — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark

en: Iceland's Elf Capital

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🧝 Hafnarfjörður
en: When the University of Iceland actually asked — first in 1974, again in 2007 — around half of Icelanders wouldn't rule out elves. This is the town where the official ones live.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🧝 Hafnarfjörður
en: ***Hafnarfjörður* = Harbour Fjord** — a Viking-age settlement and one of Iceland's top trading ports from the **15th century**, where English and Hanseatic merchants shipped out **dried cod.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🧝 Hafnarfjörður
en: The town is built **into the lava** — streets and gardens threaded through **Búrfellshraun**, a flow ~**8,000 years old.** That makes it the self-declared **elf capital of Iceland.** When the University of Iceland actually asked — first in **1974**, again in **2007** — around **half** wouldn't rule out the ***huldufólk*** (hidden people) living in the rocks. The town keeps an official **elf map**, and planners sometimes call in **elf consultants** before roadworks. The lava park **Hellisgerði** is prime hidden-folk real estate.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🧝 Hafnarfjörður
en: A carpenter called **Jóhannes Reykdal** dammed the stream behind his workshop, wired in a generator from Norway, and in the first days of **December 1904** lit about **fifteen houses** — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — and four street lamps: **Iceland's first hydroelectric station.** Reykjavík didn't manage its own until **1921.**

ctx: block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: Iceland's entire modern economy starts with that one deal: build a smelter, and to feed it, build a national power company. Everything you will see today is downstream of a Swiss handshake in 1966.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: A Saint Of Fire, Next Door To A Smelter

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: That lava has a name older than the buildings: **Nýjahraun** — "the new lava." It ran in **1151.** Iceland has been calling it *new* for **875 years**, which tells you everything about the pace of things here.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: The plant is **ISAL**, the aluminium smelter at **Straumsvík.** Built by the Swiss company **Alusuisse** under a law Alþingi passed on **13 May 1966**, it started producing in **1969** at a modest **33,000 tonnes a year.** Today it runs at about **202,000 tonnes**, with a licence for **230,000**, employs **381 people** (end of 2025) and is owned outright by **Rio Tinto.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: Here is the bit that actually matters. To run it, Iceland had to build a power station — so **Landsvirkjun was founded on 1 July 1965** and put up **Búrfellsstöð**, which started on **16 September 1969.** The smelter took **half the station's output, 105 MW.** *(In 2025 it bought **3,334 gigawatt-hours.**)* The **alumina** arrives by ship mostly from **Brazil**, the finished aluminium leaves through **Rotterdam** to around **60 customers**, and it comes out as **billet** — the stuff extruded into window frames and solar-panel rails.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: Now the lava. **Kapelluhraun** poured out of the **Krýsuvíkureldar in 1151** — the same fires we will meet again in an hour. Locals call it **Bruninn**, "the burn", and the medieval name **Nýjahraun** turns up in *Kjalnesinga saga* and in an annal entry for a **1343** shipwreck. People **watched this one arrive.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: And out there in the rock is a tiny ruin called **Kapellan**, the chapel. On **21 May 1950** it was excavated by **Kristján Eldjárn** — later President of Iceland — with three colleagues. The building was **2.4 metres long.** Inside they found, broken into three pieces, a **carved claystone figure of Saint Barbara**, about **3.3 cm** of her surviving from an original of maybe **5.5 cm**, still holding her tower. Pre-Reformation. A wayside shrine where travellers stopped to pray before crossing the lava.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: **Barbara is the patron saint of travellers — and of everyone who works with fire, metal and explosives.** She has been sitting in that lava for five hundred years, and then somebody built an aluminium smelter next door. *(She is now the most appropriately employed saint in the North Atlantic.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
en: The chapel also carries a grim story: that a man from **Bessastaðir** was killed and buried here in the reprisals after the execution of **Bishop Jón Arason.** Kristján Eldjárn dug for it and **found nothing to support it** — and said so. Good man.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: A rift-built ridge, a road built to dodge the snow, and an aquifer that ties this pass to the smelter back down the coast. Everything on this peninsula is plumbed into everything else.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: Every good Icelandic road starts life as a newspaper column explaining why it should never be built.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: The Road Everyone Said Was A Waste Of Money

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: When they proposed this road in **1936**, the newspapers took it apart. Árni Óla wrote in **1940** that the project had "mostly met with condemnation" and that this exact pass would be the most expensive and difficult stretch of the lot. **We are about to drive the argument.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: The ridge on the right is **Sveifluháls.** It was built underneath a glacier — a fissure eruption erupting into ice, quenching into **móberg**, hyaloclastite, and stacking itself into a wall instead of spreading into a plain. It runs **north-east to south-west**, which is not a coincidence: that is the direction of the rift. The whole **Krýsuvík volcanic system** is about **8 km wide and 50 km long**, and this ridge is drawn along it like a pencil line on a map.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: The road was **Jónas Jónsson and Jón Baldvinsson's** idea, put to Alþingi in **March 1936.** The pitch was weather. The existing route east crossed **Hellisheiði at 370 metres.** This one would top out at **168.** A **snow-free winter road** to the south. That was the whole argument.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: It cost a fortune, it took years, and the stretch past **Kleifarvatn** was not finished until around **1945.** *(Which means the fastest way to make an Icelander build you a road is to point out that the other one gets snowed in.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
en: One more thing you cannot see and should know. The pass is being **quarried** — for exactly the same móberg the ridge is made of. And the local objection is not about the view. **The groundwater under Undirhlíðar runs downhill and comes out at Straumsvík** — the smelter we passed twenty minutes ago. A public consultation on new extraction ran from **25 September to 6 November 2025.**

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: The Lake That Pulled Its Own Plug

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: In the year 2000 this lake started emptying. Nobody drained it, nobody dammed it. **An earthquake opened a crack in the bottom and the water simply left.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: **Kleifarvatn** is the biggest lake on the peninsula — about **10 km²**, up to **97 metres deep**, sitting roughly **140 metres above sea level** in a closed basin on the eastern edge of the **Krýsuvík fissure swarm.** Vísindavefurinn's answer is that the basin is probably part of a **caldera around 10 km across** — a collapse, not an explosion crater — and that the lake in its present form is roughly **10,000 to 12,000 years old.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: Here is the oddity: **it has no river running out of it.** Before 2000 the water drained north into **Lambhagatjörn** and then underground, all the way to the sea at **Straumsvík.** A lake that empties itself through the floor is already unusual. Then the floor got worse.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: The **earthquakes of 2000** opened and widened fissures at and near the lake's northern end, and over the **following two years the surface dropped about four metres.** Beaches appeared. The jetty ended up a long way from the water. It has since recovered a good deal, but the point stands: on this peninsula even the lakes are provisional.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: It also has a monster, and the sightings are dated. In **1749**, witnesses said they watched the thing haul itself out onto a spit and lie there for **about two hours.** By **1750** people **would not fish here at all**, though the lake was full of fish, because of *"orms eða slöngu sem væri svört að lit"* — a worm or serpent, black, reckoned to be **the size of a medium whale, thirty to forty metres long.** In **1755** something surfaced *"líkasta skötu að lit og lögun"* — closest to a skate in colour and shape, and enormous.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn
en: And when the water finally did drop, Iceland's best-selling crime writer was waiting. **Arnaldur Indriðason's *Kleifarvatn* (2004)** — published in English as ***The Draining Lake*** — opens with the falling water level uncovering **a body that had been down there for decades.** He did not have to invent the setting. He just read the news.

en: the peninsula's biggest lake, 97 m deep, no river out

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
en: The Fires That Shut The Door

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
en: This system last erupted in the twelfth century, ran for nearly forty years, and then closed for eight hundred. It has not opened since. That is either reassuring or it isn't.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
en: The **Krýsuvíkureldar of 1151 to 1188** laid down **Ögmundarhraun**, **Mávahlíðahraun** and **Kapelluhraun** — three flows that between them rewrote the south coast of this peninsula and buried at least one farm.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
en: Then the system **shut, and has stayed shut for over eight centuries.** Meanwhile its neighbours — Fagradalsfjall in 2021, Svartsengi and Sundhnúkur from 2023 — have been extremely busy. Same peninsula, same rift, completely different diaries.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
en: That is how the **Reykjanes Fires** work. The peninsula sleeps for centuries, then wakes for decades of eruptions across several systems, then sleeps again. The last full cycle ran roughly **950 to 1240 CE** and laid most of the lava we have driven on today. We are, on the current reading, at the beginning of the next one.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: Where They Drilled For The Queen And Got A Crater

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: In October 1999 a borehole here stopped blowing, thought about it for a bit, and then **exploded** — leaving a crater forty-three metres across and throwing mud seven hundred metres up the hillside.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: This is a **high-temperature geothermal field** at the heart of the Krýsuvík system, and the colours are not decoration — they are the rock being eaten. Steam rises off the deep reservoir, condenses near the surface, and brings up **carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.** Those gases turn the water acid, and the acid digests fresh lava into soft clay. **The mud you are photographing is bedrock that lost an argument with chemistry.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: Those pale yellow mounds have a name and a mechanism. **Brennisteinsþúfur** — sulphur mounds — form where **hydrogen sulphide reaches the surface and oxidises in open air**, dropping pure sulphur out of the gas. Vísindavefurinn puts them at **10 to 20 metres across and 1 to 1.5 metres high**, and — this is the good bit — **hollow inside.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: People mined that sulphur. According to the site's own panels there were two runs: **1754 to 1763**, and again **1858 to 1880**, and contemporary records have **72.5 tonnes of sulphur exported from Krýsuvík in the eighteenth century.** Sulphur meant gunpowder. This muddy field was, briefly, a strategic resource.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: And this is where Iceland's geothermal drilling starts. **Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson** bored here with a hand-turned iron drill in the **autumn of 1755 and the summer of 1756** — the first attempt anywhere in the country. *(Bjarni Pálsson is a name worth keeping: he became Iceland's first* landlæknir*, the first state physician. On the South Coast run he turns up again as Sveinn Pálsson's father-in-law.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: Fast forward two centuries. **Rafveita Hafnarfjarðar**, the Hafnarfjörður electricity utility, drilled a research hole here — remembered as **Drottningarholan**, "the Queen's Hole" — and at around **230 metres down the hole blew.** Be straight with the guests about one thing: **the sources give the year as either 1947 or 1949 and I have not been able to settle it.** What nobody disputes is what it did next.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún
en: It blew, on and off, for **half a century.** Then on **Thursday 25 October 1999** it stopped — and shortly afterwards the ground beside it detonated in a steam explosion, opening a crater **about 43 metres across** and flinging mud **700 metres to the north.** The walkways you are standing on were laid out afterwards, by people who had just watched what this ground does when it is annoyed.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: The Green Lake Nobody Can Fully Explain

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: This is the crater Icelandic geology textbooks use as **the** example of its type. It is roughly **45 metres deep** in a hole only a few hundred metres across. And the reason it is green — **the sources genuinely disagree**, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: **Grænavatn** is a **sprengigígur**, an explosion crater — blown out in a single blast where rising magma met groundwater. Vísindavefur, the University of Iceland's own science service, lists it as the type example for the whole category. Age: **somewhere around six to seven thousand years** — one source says 7,000, another says over 6,000, and nobody has narrowed it further.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: Depth: **about 45 metres**, which is the figure the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** published in **1950.** The official sign at Krýsuvík says **46.** Width: "a few hundred metres" is as precise as anyone will commit to. *(A lake nobody has bothered to measure properly, in a country that measures everything. I love it here.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: Now the colour, honestly. **Sigurður Þórarinsson wrote in 1950 that it comes from sulphur compounds in the water.** The **official information board** at the site says it comes from **geothermal algae and crystals absorbing the green light of the sun.** Both are published. Neither has been settled. Take your pick, and if a guest tells you they read something different on the internet, they are probably reading a translation of one of these two.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: The properly weird bit is in the rock thrown out of it. The tephra around Grænavatn contains **gabbro nodules** — lumps of a deep, coarse-grained rock the magma tore off on its way up. **Gabbro has not been found anywhere else in south-west Iceland.** This little hole punched through something nothing else has reached.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
en: And in a second we drive **between two more of them.** **Augun** — "the Eyes" — are two small water-filled craters, one on each side of the road, sitting on their own **300-metre crater row.** There are at least **four separate rows** in this cluster, and **Gestsstaðavatn** to the west is the oldest. This is not one volcano. It is a small committee of them.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: The Church That Burned Down And Was Built Again By Apprentices

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: That church burned to the ground in the small hours of **2 January 2010.** The fire brigade got the call at **02:04** and by the time they arrived **the building had already fallen.** What you are looking at is an **exact replica**, built by carpentry students — and the altarpiece inside is **the original.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: The church that burned was built in **1857** by **Beinteinn Stefánsson**, a tenant farmer and carpenter at Arnarfell, out of **driftwood.** It stopped being a parish church around **1910**, was formally abolished in **1917**, and in **1929** it was deconsecrated and turned into somebody's house. Rebuilt and reconsecrated on **Whit Sunday, 31 May 1964**, taken into the care of the **National Museum** that same year, and legally protected on **1 January 1990.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: Then the fire. It was **arson** — a man in his early twenties was later given a **one-year suspended sentence** for setting it alight. Twenty years of protected status, gone in under an hour.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: Here is the part I like. The replacement was built by the **carpentry school in Hafnarfjörður** — Iðnskólinn, later Tækniskólinn — working with the **National Museum** and a volunteer society, deliberately as a **teaching project in old timber technique.** The insurance payout from the old church bought the materials. It is an **exact copy** and it **seats 40.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: It came back on **9 October 2020**, and could not be lifted onto the old foundation that day because the wind got up. They craned it into place **the next morning.** COVID then delayed the consecration by nearly two years, until **Whit Sunday, 5 June 2022, at two o'clock.** It now belongs to the parish in **Hafnarfjörður.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: And the altarpiece. It was painted for this church by **Sveinn Björnsson** — who was a painter *and* the **chief detective of Hafnarfjörður**, which is a combination I have never encountered anywhere else. Every autumn, after the September service, the picture was taken down and **stored in Hafnarfjarðarkirkja for the winter.** Which is exactly where it was on the night of 2 January 2010. **The painting survived the fire because of a filing habit.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
en: Sveinn died in **1997** and is buried in that churchyard — the **first burial there since 1917**, and the last. At the 2022 consecration they poured communion wine on his grave.

en: Twelve eruptions in four years, then thirteen months of silence with the ground still swelling underneath. This is not the end of anything. It is the gap between two paragraphs.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Twelve Eruptions And Counting

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Some of the lava we are about to walk on is younger than most of the phones on this bus.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: After **1240 the peninsula went quiet for about 800 years** — then on **19 March 2021** a fissure split open at **Fagradalsfjall** and the Fires restarted. That first show ran six months; **more than 50,000 people** hiked out to watch a volcano like it was a gig.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Then **Meradalir (2022)** and **Litli-Hrútur** ("Little Ram", **2023**), before the action jumped north to the **Sundhnúkur crater row** by Grindavík. **Veðurstofa Íslands counts nine eruptions there.** The ninth began on **16 July 2025** and the Met Office **formally declared it over on 5 August 2025.** That is **twelve eruptions on this peninsula since 2021.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: **And then it stopped.** As of **18 August 2026** Veðurstofan's line is *"Kvikusöfnun og landris heldur áfram við Svartsengi"* — **magma accumulation and uplift are continuing at Svartsengi**, at a rate that has held steady for weeks. Around **ten small earthquakes a day**, most of them north of Grindavík. **No eruption since the fifth of August last year** — which makes today, as we drive across it, **thirteen months of quiet.** The longest pause of the whole series.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Be careful how you say the next part, because it is the honest one. **The ground is still rising. The magma is still arriving. The Met Office's own assessment is that a new dike intrusion, and possibly a new eruption, remains the most likely outcome.** *(For the exact volume under Svartsengi and today's hazard-zone colours — check vedur.is this morning. Those numbers move and a stale one is worse than none.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: **"Could it go off while we're here?"** You will get asked. The honest answer: it could. Here is what matters — when the magma moves it goes **sideways first**, and that dike run is the warning. **Veðurstofa Íslands puts the historic range at twenty minutes to just over four hours.** Iceland has evacuated this ground repeatedly and has **not lost a single person to lava.** If it happens today we will know before it reaches the surface, and we will be somewhere else.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Two footnotes for the geology-curious. **Kristján Sæmundsson** and **Magnús Á. Sigurgeirsson** describe **Fagradalsfjall** as unlike anything else on the peninsula — **no central volcano, no proper fissure swarm, no high-temperature field**, roughly **5 km wide and 15 km long.** Its **picrite** comes up fast and from deep without loitering in a magma chamber, which is exactly why nothing filled slowly where the instruments could watch it. And the valley the 2021 fissure opened in, **Geldingadalir**, means the **wether valleys** — named for **castrated rams**, because sheep came there for a mouthful of grass. **Hallgrímur J. Ámundason** settled that at **Vísindavefurinn** on **24 March 2021**, five days into the eruption, from the place-name register of the farm **Hraun** in Grindavík.
